translatedData.subTitle:
Where you place your stop-loss takes more thought than whether to use one at all. Place it too close and you’ll get stopped out every day; too far away and one loss can wipe you out.

【Fixed-percentage method】For example, exit whenever you lose 1%–2% of your capital. Simple and straightforward—good for beginners
to build discipline. The downside is that it ignores market structure, so your stop might land right in a cluster of other traders’ stop-losses.

【Technical-level stop-loss method】Place it where the market structure is invalidated: for a long position, below key support; for a short position,
above resistance. The logic is: if the price breaks through this level, it’s evidence that I was wrong.

[State 1: Funding rates stay strongly positive] This means longs are crowded, and everyone is borrowing money to go long. At this point, the market
is often accelerating toward a top, and could plunge sharply at any moment in a long squeeze. I’m not telling you to immediately
short; rather, be especially cautious about chasing longs at this stage, and tighten your stop-loss.

[State 2: Funding rates stay negative] Shorts are crowded. Extremely negative funding rates often appear near panic-driven bottoms,
because everyone who needed to get out has already done so, yet people are still shorting. Many major rallies in the past have started at times like these.

translatedData.title: What Is the Funding Rate? Why Do Longs Pay Shorts?
translatedData.subTitle:
There’s one term you can’t avoid when trading perpetual contracts: the funding rate. It’s settled every 8 hours, and it’s a payment between longs and shorts.
The two sides pay each other; the exchange only collects and distributes the money—it doesn’t profit from it.

【How it works】Perpetual contracts have no expiration date, so how does their price stay in line with the spot price? That’s where the funding rate comes in:
When the contract price is higher than the spot price (bullish sentiment) → the funding rate is positive → longs pay shorts;
When the contract price is lower than the spot price (bears have the upper hand) → the funding rate is negative → shorts pay longs.
The money flows back and forth between both sides, pulling the contract price toward the spot price.
